label: Seeing people
rationale: Getting together: meeting up with a friend, seeing someone home, going back to your parents', and birthdays.
mixUps: au takes ni (tomodachi ni au), not o. Seeing someone home is okuru (okutte iku yo), not tsurete iku. jikka ni kaeru is going back to your parents' place, while uchi ni kaeru is just going home.

targets.trap: English 'meet a friend' or 'see a friend' leads to tomodachi o au or tomodachi o miru. People you meet take ni or to (tomodachi ni au, tomodachi to au), and miru with a person means watching or minding them (kodomo mitete = keep an eye on the kids).
targets.use: The everyday way to say what you're doing on a day off: kyou wa tomodachi ni au (I'm seeing a friend today). tomodachi to au is also heard and stresses a meet-up you both arranged; asobu (hang out) is the other weekend verb.
targets.notes: Bumping into a friend by chance is also au: eki de guuzen atta.

example.romaji: ashita tomodachi ni au n da.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa tomodachi ni au n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は友達に会うんです。

targets.verbSense: send; also see someone off or take them somewhere
targets.trap: English 'take you home' leads to tsurete iku, which sounds like leading someone who can't go alone (a child, a drunk friend). Seeing someone home as a courtesy, on foot or by car, is okuru: okutteku yo.
partners: genkan (the front door: genkan made okuru = see someone to the door)
targets.use: The offer at the end of an evening is okutteku yo (I'll walk or drive you home), often without naming the place, and the thanks is okutte kurete arigatou. made marks how far you go: eki made okuru (see someone to the station). The one taken home says uchi, their own home: uchi made okutte kureta (they saw me home).
targets.notes: miokuru is seeing someone off at the door, station or airport.

example.romaji: osoi kara, ie made okutteku yo.
example.ja: 遅いから、家まで送ってくよ。
example.english: It's late, I'll see you home.

examplePolite.romaji: osoi node, ie made okurimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 遅いので、家まで送りますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's late, so I'll take you home.

targets.verbSense: go back to where you belong (home, your country)
targets.trap: English 'go to my parents' place' leads to oya no uchi ni iku, which sounds like a visit. The home you grew up in is jikka, and you kaeru to it. Your spouse's family home takes iku: tsuma no jikka ni iku.
partners: inaka (your home region in the country)
targets.use: The holiday question and answer: oshougatsu wa jikka ni kaeru? (going home for New Year?), obon wa jikka kaeru yo. It takes kaeru because it's a return, even after years of living away.
targets.notes: satogaeri = a trip back to your family home, also a mother-to-be going home to give birth.

example.romaji: oshougatsu wa jikka ni kaeru no?
example.ja: お正月は実家に帰るの？
example.english: Are you going home for New Year?

examplePolite.romaji: oshougatsu wa jikka ni kaerimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お正月は実家に帰りますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you going back to your family's for New Year?

targets.kana: たんじょうびをいわう
targets.use: Mostly about others doing it for or with you: minna ga tanjoubi iwatte kureta (everyone celebrated my birthday), or planning: kanojo no tanjoubi, dou iwaou? The greeting itself is tanjoubi omedetou.
targets.notes: oiwai suru is the softer noun form: tanjoubi no oiwai shiyou (let's do something for the birthday).

example.romaji: minna ga tanjoubi iwatte kureta n da.
example.ja: みんなが誕生日祝ってくれたんだ。
example.english: Everyone celebrated my birthday for me.

examplePolite.romaji: minna ga tanjoubi o iwatte kureta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: みんなが誕生日を祝ってくれたんです。

reviewPool.english: suit someone, look good on someone
not suit someone, can't make it (a time)
